content: A Community Health Center is dedicated to enhancing the health and well-being of the population it serves. Health is comprehensively defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, rather than merely the absence of disease or infirmity. To achieve optimal health outcomes, community health services prioritize prevention, early intervention, rehabilitation, and education, alongside the provision of direct care. Community health services engage in a variety of activities, including the delivery of specialized services such as podiatry, counseling, and physiotherapy, which are offered both at clinical offices and through outreach programs. They also focus on health promotion and education, case management, advocacy, and targeted interventions. Furthermore, these services foster collaborative relationships with industries, government entities, hospitals, and other healthcare providers to ensure a comprehensive approach to community health. Community health services play a critical role within the healthcare sector. They are essential in promoting and maintaining well-being and good health, particularly for individuals and groups who face financial barriers to accessing care. These services are grounded in long-term efforts that embody principles such as empowerment, accessibility for marginalized populations, community partnerships, and the delivery of client-centered, integrated, and multidisciplinary care. Community Health Centers that receive federal funding through the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) under the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) are designated as Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs). Currently, there are over 4,000 federally supported service delivery sites, including community health centers, migrant health centers, healthcare for the homeless centers, and public housing primary care centers. These facilities provide high-quality primary and preventive healthcare to more than 15 million individuals across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and the Pacific Basin. Over the years, health centers have established a strong track record of delivering high-quality preventive and primary care to millions of low-income residents in urban inner cities and remote rural areas. In 2002, President George W. Bush launched the Health Centers Initiative, which aimed to significantly expand access to primary healthcare services in 1,200 communities through the establishment of new or expanded health center sites. This initiative resulted in a nearly 50% increase in the number of patients served within five years, reaching 7 million additional individuals. By 2006, the number of patients served by health centers surpassed 15 million for the first time. Approximately two-thirds of health center patients are from minority populations, and 90% of patients have incomes below 200% of the federal poverty line. Additionally, four out of ten health center patients lack health insurance coverage. In fiscal year 2007, the federal government allocated $1.99 billion to support these vital health services.
